plate_findings.evidence: Alopecia over scalp, eyebrows, lower eyelid sparing upper eyelid
Involvement of trunk in the form of ichthyosis with erythema and brownish adherent scaling

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Infant face showing alopecia of scalp, eyebrows and lower eyelid, a classic cutaneous feature of KID syndrome in an article titled on an infant with KID syndrome. B: Trunk ichthyosis with erythema and brownish adherent scaling, consistent with the ichthyotic erythrokeratoderma plaques of KID syndrome. C: Perianal hyperkeratotic brownish plaque, a hyperkeratotic plaque manifestation of KID syndrome ichthyosis. D: Stippled keratoderma of the sole is the characteristic palmoplantar keratoderma of KID syndrome. E: Symmetrical erythematous macerated plaques of both groins in the same KID syndrome infant; flexural involvement is a recognized but less highlighted manifestation, so the finding is recorded as a proposed term.

Hypotrichosis of the eyelashes and eyebrows; aged facial appearance

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Case 1 clinical photo of plantar keratoderma, a classic KID syndrome manifestation; article title confirms KID syndrome. B: Case 1 rippled hyperkeratotic plaques on knees, characteristic KID syndrome skin finding. C: Case 1 facial photo showing sparse eyebrows/eyelashes and thickened facial skin, typical of KID syndrome. D: Case 1 eye photo showing vascularizing keratitis, a defining feature of KID syndrome (the keratitis component). E: Case 2 palmar hyperkeratosis, classic KID syndrome palmoplantar keratoderma. F: Case 2 scalp showing alopecia with ichthyosiform erythrokeratoderma, characteristic KID syndrome.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, G). A: Panel A shows the patient's characteristic skin lesions typical of KID syndrome, matching the description in the caption and text. B: Panel B displays characteristic skin lesions on the hands, consistent with KID syndrome. C: Panel C shows the progression of KID syndrome with intense erythema and the development of healthy-looking spots, as detailed in the caption. D: Panel D demonstrates the expansion and spread of healthy-looking skin over time, a recognized feature of KID progression. E: Panel E depicts the slow expansion of healthy-looking skin on the arm, aligning with the described progression of KID syndrome. G: Histological evidence (Masson's stain) shows the characteristic epidermal change (hyperkeratosis/granulosis) evolving toward normal skin, supporting the diagnosis of KID syndrome.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Panel A shows a dark brown, thick, plate-like hyperkeratotic scaling pattern on the back, which is a characteristic cutaneous finding of KID syndrome. B: Panel B displays similar thick, dark hyperkeratotic scaling on the chest and upper limbs, supporting the diagnosis of KID syndrome. C: Panel C illustrates shiny, brown-yellow skin and fissuring, particularly around joints, which are common skin findings in the course of KID syndrome. D: Panel D shows thin, flaky hyperkeratoses on the foot, another characteristic manifestation of KID syndrome. E: Panel E displays craniofacial dysmorphic features, including eclabium and eyelid ectropion, consistent with the complex clinical picture of KID syndrome. F: Panel F illustrates claw hand deformities and pseudocontractures due to skin tightening, indicating the musculoskeletal involvement often associated with KID syndrome.

panels.figure_caption: Cutaneous, craniofacial, and musculoskeletal findings in a patient with KID syndrome. (A) Dark brown, thick, plate-like hyperkeratotic scales over the back. (B) Similar scales on anterior chest and upper limbs. (C) Shiny, brown-yellow skin with fissuring at large joints (knees, elbows), indicating impaired mobility. (D) Thin, flaky hyperkeratosis over the dorsum of the foot. (E) Bilateral upper eyelid ectropion, shortened lower eyelids, flattened nasal bridge, and eclabium. (F) Claw hand deformities and pseudocontractures due to skin tightening, limiting joint range of motion.
in_text_mentions: Two weeks post-discharge, the membrane had fully desquamated, revealing thick, dark brown, plate-like hyperkeratotic scales, predominantly involving the back, limbs, and large joints (Figs. 2A–C). Thin, flaky hyperkeratosis was also observed on the face, scalp, and extremities (Fig. 2D), with relative sparing of the face and abdomen. The patient exhibited heat intolerance requiring frequent exfoliation and had rapid nail growth, necessitating regular trimming. The mother also reported photophobia and delayed tooth eruption, with dentition beginning at age 2.

On examination, the patient exhibited bilateral upper eyelid ectropion, shortened lower eyelids, a flat nasal bridge, eclabium (fish-like mouth), and hypodontia (Fig. 2E). Her skin was parchment-like with a shiny brown hue and prominent fissuring, particularly at joint and flexural areas (Fig. 2C). Claw hand deformities and pseudocontractures were noted, resulting in joint stiffness and limited mobility (Fig. 2F). Deep tendon reflexes were absent. The limbs were normally formed with an appropriate number of digits.
